newsitem.title: USA: Capitol police face runoff in first-ever union race.
newsitem.headline: Capitol police face runoff in first-ever union race.

text.p: U.S. Capitol Police held their first-ever union election Wednesday, after much legal wrangling and delay, but failed to select a clear winner to represent the special force that protects federal lawmakers.

The Teamsters garnered the most votes in the balloting, 203, followed by the Fraternal Order of Police, 180, and the International Union of Police Associations, 154, according to union officials. Turnout was 84 percent.
Because no union won a clear majority a runoff must be held between the top two vote getters in coming weeks.
Complicating the situation, 50 of the ballots cast were challenged by unions and police officials, which officials said made it unclear who would be in the runoff.
The Teamsters were not as uncertain.
"As far as we're concerned, the challenged ballots won't alter the outcome," said Patrick Lacefield of the Teamsters, who said his union expected to face off against the FOP.

The Capitol police force did not have the right to a union election until two years ago when congressional Republicans passed legislation to make Congress, which had long exempted itself, comply with federal labour and workplace laws.
The road to the election, which began Tuesday, was paved with problems. Police officials resisted calls for a union, saying officers were involved in national security work.
And two years after the law was passed it was still unclear how many other Capitol Hill staffers will be allowed to join unions.
